spans.content: Detection of Dobrava-Belgrade hantavirus using recombinant-
nucleocapsid-based enzyme-linked immunosorbent assay
and SYBR Green-based real-time reverse transcriptase-
polymerase chain reaction
Vikto´ria Ne´meth

Received: 18 January 2011 / Accepted: 27 April 2011 / Published online: 14 May 2011
Springer-Verlag 2011
Abstract Dobrava (DOBV) hantaviruses belong to the
genus Hantavirus, family Bunyaviridae, and are carried by
yellow-necked and striped field mice. The goal of this
study was to detect DOBV using serological and genetic
methods in Apodemus rodents in Hungary and in northern
Croatia. During the study period, a total of 125 Apodemus
sp. (67 A. agrarius, 58 A. flavicollis) were tested for the
presence of hantaviruses, and 21 rodents
were
positive by rRT-PCR and/or ELISA. We conclude that the
prevalence of DOBV is much higher than previously
anticipated. The simultaneous use of molecular and sero-
logical techniques provides a highly reliable way to detect
hantavirus infections.

Introduction
Hantaviruses (HTV, family Bunyaviridae, genus Hantavi-
rus) are enveloped, negative-sense single-stranded RNA
viruses that infect a variety of rodents. HTVs spread
between rodents and humans through direct contact or by
the aerosolized excreta (urine, feces and saliva) of infected
animals. The clinical picture of hemorrhagic fever with
renal syndrome (HFRS) and nephropathia epidemica (NE)
occurs in several countries in Europe and Asia. In Europe,
five major serotypes had been identified, i.e., Dobrava-
Belgrade (DOBV), Puumala (PUUV), Saaremaa (SAAV),
Seoul (SEOV) and Tula (TULV) viruses, with PUUV being
the most common serotype, carried mainly by bank voles
(Myodes glareolus). DOBV and SAAV are carried by
yellow-necked (Apodemus flavicollis) and striped field
(Apodemus agrarius) mice, respectively [3, 16, 18]. Pre-
vious epizootiological studies of small mammals captured
in HFRS-endemic regions have suggested that shrews
(order Soricomorpha, family Soricidae) and moles (family
Talpidae) might also serve as reservoir hosts of HTVs [2, 6,
17]. For several years, there has been a disagreement
regarding the taxonomy of DOBV hantaviruses. When
SAAV was first identified [14], it was considered a genetic
variant of DOBV. The International Committee on Tax-
onomy of Viruses (ICTV) declares that SAAV is a distinct
virus species rather than a lineage of DOBV. However, it
has been surmised that DOBV, which is one of the most
common hantaviruses in central and southeastern Europe,
has three characterized lineages according to their specific
rodent hosts, Apodemus flavicollis, A. agrarius and
A. ponticus. The corresponding virus lineages are proposed
as DOBV-Af, DOBV-Aa, and DOBV-Ap, respectively [12,
13]. Hence, it might be assumed that not all A. agrarius-
associated sequences detected in Central Europe are

necessarily closely related to SAAV. DOBV and PUUV are
the two major serotypes circulating and causing human
diseases in Hungary [5, 7, 8, 15]; however, Tula virus
(TULV), Nova virus (NVAV) and Seewis virus (SWSV)
have also been detected [9–11]. The aims of this study
were to express a truncated form of DOBV nucleocapsid
protein and using this recombinant antigen (in an ELISA)
along with the SYBR Green-based real-time reverse tran-
scription-polymerase chain reaction (rRT-PCR) method for
detection of DOBV carried by Apodemus rodents in Hun-
gary and northern Croatia.
Materials and methods
Apodemus sp. were tested for the presence of hantavirus.
As part of an ecological study run in parallel, animals were
trapped in seven different locations of the Transdanubian
region of Hungary (Somogy, Zala and Baranya Counties)
and northern Croatia (near Gola and Beli Manastir vil-
lages), during the summer and autumn seasons of
2005-2007. Rodents were live-trapped; each capture trap
was checked two times per day (evening and morning).
Due to the ecological study, animals that perished naturally
in the trap were used for the virology studies only. Animals
were identified by an expert taxonomist and all data from
the specimens were collected in a computer database.
Lung, kidney, spleen, liver and heart tissue samples of
dissected rodents were removed and stored at

Based on the study previously published by Araki et al.
[1], a truncated form of DOBV nucleocapsid protein
(rNP50) was produced with an Escherichia coli expression
system, using newly detected DOBV strain (DOB/Pe´cs/
242Af/06). The part of the NP gene of this strain encoding
amino acids 50 to 429 was amplified, and the fragment was
then cloned into the
6 \times
His-tagged prokaryotic expression
vector pET28a (Novagene) following the manufacturer’s
recommendations. E. coli BL21 Rosetta (DE3) pLysS
competent cells were transformed with the recombinant
pET28a-DOBV-rNP50 plasmid. Proteins were purified
from the lysed BL21 cells using HIS Select HF Nickel
Affinity Gel (Sigma). The concentration of the eluted
protein was determined via spectrophotometry using the
Bradford assay (Sigma) according to the manufacturer’s
instructions.
In order to verify the protein activity, standard western
blot (WB) analyses were performed using antibodies
against
6 \times
His-tag (Penta-His monoclonal antibody,
QIAGEN) and DOBV nucleoprotein protein collected from
a DOBV-infected human patient (RG06).
Rodent blood samples were screened for the presence of
antibodies against DOBV by standard indirect enzyme-
linked immunosorbent assay (ELISA) using rNP50
( 0 . 5 ~ \mu \mathrm { g }
per well) as antigen and HRP-conjugated goat anti-mouse
(1:5000; Millipore) antibody as secondary antibody.
Specimens were considered positive if the absorbance in
the sample wells was equal to or greater than three times
the mean value of that of a panel of negative control sera
derived form the same species. In order to evaluate our
ELISA method properly, specificity and sensitivity were
determined. A commercially available DOBV- and Han-
taan (HNTV)-specific ELISA (Reagena) was used as the
reference detection method. Eight DOBV-IgG-positive and
42 HTV-negative serum samples collected previously from
patients hospitalized with suspected HTV infection were
randomly selected. All ELISAs carried out in order to
calculate specificity and sensitivity were performed blinded
by an independent person. The chi-squared test was used to
analyze the results.

Discussion
A truncated nucleocapsid protein, DOBV rNP50, expressed
in E. coli, was used to detect antibodies against hantavi-
ruses in rodents collected in Hungary and Croatia. A
pET28a vector is a bacterial plasmid designed to enable the
quick production of any protein in large quantities within a
host cell. Using rNP50 in an ELISA system is not new,
Araki et al. [1] previously expressed this protein in
recombinant baculovirus. We only adopted their concept
and optimized the expression in an E. coli system, which is
more accessible for standard molecular biological or viro-
logical laboratories. They concluded that the first 49 amino
acids at the N-terminal of the HTV NP contains immuno-
dominant and linear epitopes. Truncated rNP lacking these
amino acids is a useful protein for serotyping and for dif-
ferentiating antibodies against DOBV, HNTV and SEOV
[1]. The ELISA test we developed provided results com-
parable to those of a commercially available test for
detecting DOBV-specific antibodies, with specificity and
sensitivity as high as
and

on these results, we surmise that the truncated form of the
protein does not significantly decrease the sensitivity of the
rNP50-based assay. Hence, the relatively high number of
rRT-PCR-positive but ELISA-negative serum samples is
not likely to be the result of the novel ELISA with lower

South Transdanubian and North Croatian region. Based on
these results showing discrepancies between serology and
rRT-PCR, we conclude that it is necessary to use molecular
and serological analyses in parallel to get a more accurate
estimate of HTV incidence. In the majority of the previous
studies, only serologically positive samples were further
tested by molecular methods, likely causing the incidence
of HTV to be underestimated. To explain the apparent
discrepancies between the results of the serological and
molecular approaches, we offer the following scenario:
After infection, virus particles are present in the lung for
about a two-week period (acute phase); i.e., a period in
which PCR detection is the method to provide a reliable
result (Fig. 3). It is likely, however, that immunological
reactions do not produce a strong response in the acute
phase, making ELISA tests frequently negative. During the
first half of the persistent phase, however, antibody pro-
duction increases. Although this is likely to be accompanied
by a decreasing virus load in the lungs, it still might be suf-
ficient for rRT-PCR detection. In the second half of the
persistent phase, the number of virus particles can decrease
below the threshold of detectability by PCR, whereas
antibody titers remain high [4]. Consequently, we surmise
that there might be PCR-positive animals among the sero-
logically negative ones in these previous studies as well.
On the other hand, the high prevalence of HTVs in the
trapping area is only partly informative, since the data were
collected in different seasons and locations during a three-
year period. However, it might be emphasized that a large
number of HTV-infected rodents in the region may serve as
important data, not only for researchers but also for phy-
sicians, due to the risk for human exposure.
With both A. agrarius and A. flavicollis being abundant
species in Europe, and hence in Hungary, the higher
prevalence of DOBV was expected in the area of the sur-
vey. In a recent paper, Plyusnina et al. [15] investigated the
prevalence of DOBV, SAAV and PUUV in Hungary. Of

methods, and/or the fact that rodent trapping was carried

In the present study, we detect and estimate the preva-
lence of DOBV circulating among Apodemus mice in the
Transdanubian region of Hungary and in northern Croatia,
using serologic (ELISA) and molecular detection (rRT-
PCR) methods. To our best knowledge, this is the first
study in which recombinant-viral-protein-based ELISA
was used to detect HTVs in rodent samples in Hungary and
northern Croatia. Based on our results, we conclude that
HTV infections might occur more often as expected before,
and in order to survey HTV infections, it is necessary to use
molecular and serological analyses in parallel.
